newsitem.title: USA: FCC chief revises universal phone plan.
newsitem.headline: FCC chief revises universal phone plan.

text.p: The top U.S. communications regulator proposed Tuesday to slash the size of a planned multi-billion-dollar federal fund that would subsidise phone service in high-cost rural areas and low-income neighbourhoods.

Responding to objections by state regulators, Federal Communications Commission Chairman Reed Hundt suggested the federal "universal service" programme be financed solely by tapping the interstate revenues of phone carriers.
A joint board of federal and state regulators had proposed last November to fund the programme by using both interstate and intrastate revenues. Some state regulators opposed that plan.
Hundt had estimated such a joint fund would total anywhere from $10 billion to $20 billion. He told reporters Tuesday the new federal fund he envisions would "clearly be single-digit."
Hundt, following a speech to a group of state regulators, said his new proposal would mean a smaller federal pot for subsidising high-cost phone service around the nation.
But states would have more of their own money to finance universal service programmes at the state level. "We'll do our part. And they'll have to do their part," Hundt said.
Historically the FCC share in subsidising universal service had amounted to about 25 percent while the states' proportion totalled the remaining 75 percent.
When the existing proposal was announced last fall, some state officials had argued states should have control over the dollars derived from intrastate phone traffic.
"I don't want to have a jurisdictional civil war about this," Hundt said after his speech to the National Association of Regulatory and Utility Commissioners.
